docs: How a Model Writes an Answer

chunks.text: A language model never sees letters or whole sentences directly. Before any processing, text is split into small pieces called tokens. A token is often a word, part of a word, or a punctuation mark. For example, "unbelievable" might become three tokens: "un", "believ", and "able". A rough rule of thumb for English is that one token is about four characters, or about three quarters of a word.

chunks.section: Why not just use words or letters?
chunks.text: Using whole words would need an enormous vocabulary and could not handle new words, typos, or names. Using single letters would make sequences very long and slow to process. Subword tokens are a compromise: common words get a single token, while rare words are built from smaller pieces. The most common method for building this vocabulary is called Byte Pair Encoding (BPE), which repeatedly merges the most frequent pairs of characters into new tokens.

Each token in the vocabulary has a number called its token ID. The model actually works with these numbers, not with text. The sentence "I like cats" might become a list such as [40, 588, 19987]. When the model writes an answer, it produces token IDs one at a time, which are then turned back into text.

The context window is the maximum number of tokens a model can look at in one go. It includes the instructions, any documents, the conversation so far, and the answer being written. If something does not fit in the context window, the model cannot see it at all. This limit is one of the main reasons Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) exists: instead of pasting a whole library into the prompt, we retrieve only the most relevant pieces.
AI services usually charge per token, and speed is measured in tokens per second. Languages other than English, code, and unusual words often use more tokens for the same amount of meaning.

An embedding is a list of numbers (a vector) that represents the meaning of a piece of text. A small embedding model might turn any sentence into a list of 384 numbers. Texts with similar meanings get vectors that point in similar directions, even if they use completely different words. "How do I fix a flat tyre?" and "repairing a punctured bike wheel" end up close together.

Imagine a giant map where every sentence is a dot. Sentences about cooking cluster in one region, sentences about football in another, and sentences about space travel somewhere else. An embedding is the coordinates of a sentence on that map. Real embeddings have hundreds of dimensions instead of two, which is impossible to picture, so visualizers squash them down to 2D using techniques like Principal Component Analysis (PCA). Squashing loses information, so distances on a 2D picture are only approximate.

To compare two embeddings we usually use cosine similarity. It measures the angle between two vectors: a score near 1 means they point the same way (very similar meaning), a score near 0 means they are unrelated. Cosine similarity ignores the length of the vectors and only cares about direction.

Embedding models are neural networks trained on huge numbers of text pairs. During training they are rewarded for placing related pairs (a question and its answer, a title and its article) close together and unrelated pairs far apart. This is called contrastive learning.

Embeddings power semantic search, recommendation systems, clustering of documents, duplicate detection, and the retrieval step of RAG systems. They are much cheaper to compute than running a full large language model.

An artificial neural network is made of simple units called neurons arranged in layers. Each neuron takes some numbers in, multiplies each by a weight, adds them up with a bias, and passes the result through an activation function such as ReLU, which simply turns negative numbers into zero. The output of one layer becomes the input of the next.

The weights are the adjustable numbers inside the network. A large language model can have billions of them. Everything the model "knows" is stored implicitly in these weights. There is no database of facts inside; knowledge is spread across many weights in a way that is hard to read directly.

Running an input through all the layers to get an output is called a forward pass. For a language model, the input is a sequence of tokens and the output is a probability for every possible next token.

Early layers tend to detect simple patterns, while deeper layers combine them into more abstract concepts. In image networks, early layers find edges and later layers find faces. In language models, early layers handle spelling and grammar while later layers handle meaning and reasoning-like patterns.
Parameters (weights and biases) are learned during training. Hyperparameters, such as the number of layers, the learning rate, or the batch size, are chosen by humans before training starts.

Almost every modern large language model is a transformer, an architecture introduced in the 2017 paper "Attention Is All You Need". A transformer is a stack of identical blocks. Each block contains an attention layer, which lets tokens share information with each other, and a feed-forward layer, which processes each token on its own.

Attention lets each token decide which other tokens are most relevant to it. In the sentence "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired", attention helps the word "it" focus strongly on "animal" rather than "street". Each token creates three vectors: a query (what am I looking for?), a key (what do I contain?), and a value (what information do I pass on?). The query of one token is compared with the keys of all other tokens to produce attention weights, which are then used to mix together their values.

Transformers run several attention operations in parallel, called heads. Different heads can specialise: one might track grammar, another might link pronouns to nouns, another might follow quotation marks.
Attention on its own does not know the order of tokens. Transformers add positional encodings so the model knows that "dog bites man" is different from "man bites dog".

Unlike older recurrent networks, which read text one word at a time, transformers process all tokens in parallel during training. This makes them much faster to train on modern GPUs, which allowed researchers to scale them to enormous sizes.

A large language model starts with random weights. During pretraining it reads a huge amount of text and repeatedly tries to predict the next token. Each time it guesses wrong, a loss function measures how wrong it was, and the weights are nudged slightly to make the right answer more likely next time. After trillions of these tiny updates, the model becomes very good at predicting text, and along the way it picks up grammar, facts, and patterns of reasoning.

The method used to nudge the weights is gradient descent. Backpropagation calculates, for every weight, which direction to move it to reduce the loss. The learning rate controls how big each step is: too large and training becomes unstable, too small and it takes forever.

After pretraining, a model is good at continuing text but not necessarily at following instructions. Fine-tuning trains it further on examples of good conversations, such as a question followed by a helpful answer.

Models are then often improved using feedback on their answers. In reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), people compare pairs of answers, a reward model learns their preferences, and the language model is trained to produce answers that score highly. Some approaches use a written set of principles, sometimes called a constitution, to guide this feedback.

A model only knows about the world up to the point its training data was collected. This is called the knowledge cutoff. To answer questions about newer or private information, a model needs that information supplied in its prompt, which is exactly what RAG does.

chunks.doc: How a Model Writes an Answer
chunks.text: A language model generates text autoregressively: it predicts one token, appends it to the input, and then predicts the next one, over and over. That is why answers appear word by word when they are streamed.

chunks.doc: How a Model Writes an Answer
chunks.text: At each step the model outputs a score called a logit for every token in its vocabulary. A softmax function turns these scores into probabilities that add up to 1. The model might say "Paris" has a 92% chance of coming next, "the" 3%, and so on.

chunks.doc: How a Model Writes an Answer
chunks.text: Choosing the next token from these probabilities is called sampling. Temperature controls how adventurous the choice is. A low temperature makes the model almost always pick the most likely token, which gives focused, repeatable answers. A high temperature flattens the probabilities, so less likely tokens get picked more often, which gives more varied and creative but less reliable text. Top-p (nucleus) sampling only considers the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p.

chunks.doc: How a Model Writes an Answer
chunks.text: Generation stops when the model produces a special end-of-turn token, or when it reaches the maximum number of tokens allowed for the answer.

chunks.doc: How a Model Writes an Answer
chunks.text: Some modern models can produce internal reasoning before their final answer. Spending more tokens reasoning step by step often improves accuracy on hard problems such as maths and coding, at the cost of more time and tokens.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation combines a search system with a language model. Instead of relying only on what the model memorised during training, a RAG system first looks up relevant documents and then gives them to the model along with the question. The model writes its answer using that supplied material. It is like an open-book exam instead of a closed-book one.

Documents are split into smaller passages called chunks, often a few hundred words each, sometimes with a small overlap so that sentences at the edges are not cut off from their context. Chunks that are too large dilute the meaning; chunks that are too small lose context.
Each chunk is turned into an embedding and stored in an index, often a vector database. This happens once, ahead of time.

When a question arrives, it is embedded with the same model. The system compares the question's vector with every chunk's vector, usually with cosine similarity, and picks the top-k most similar chunks.
The retrieved chunks are pasted into the prompt, together with instructions such as "answer using only the sources below and cite them".
The language model reads the prompt and writes an answer grounded in the sources, ideally citing which chunk each claim came from.

RAG lets a model answer questions about private, recent, or specialised information without retraining it. It reduces hallucinations because the model has the facts in front of it, and it makes answers checkable because they can point to sources. Its weak spot is retrieval itself: if the right chunk is not retrieved, the model cannot use it.

A hallucination is when an AI model states something false with confidence, such as inventing a quote, a statistic, or a book that does not exist. It happens because the model is trained to produce likely-sounding text, and a plausible-sounding falsehood can look just as likely as the truth.

The model has no built-in fact-checker. If its training data was thin on a topic, or the question is about something after its knowledge cutoff, it may fill the gap with a guess. Ambiguous questions and pressure to always give an answer make this worse.

Grounding the model in real sources with RAG, asking it to cite those sources, allowing it to say "I don't know", and checking important facts independently all help. Lower sampling temperature can also make answers more conservative.

Models learn from human-written text, which contains human biases. Without care, a model can repeat stereotypes or present one viewpoint as the only one. Developers test for and reduce bias, but no model is perfectly neutral.

chunks.section: Using AI well as a student
chunks.text: Treat AI as a study partner, not an oracle. Ask it to explain its reasoning, check claims against your textbook or trusted sources, and use it to understand ideas rather than to replace your own thinking.
